title: Given an array of integers, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. Aim for O(n log n).
shortTitle: Longest Increasing Subsequence: O(n log n) patience sort
keyPoints: Maintain a tails array where tails[k] holds the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1
For each number, binary-search for the first tail >= the number; replace it or append if none found
The tails array is always sorted, which is what makes binary search valid
The length of the tails array equals the LIS length, but tails is not the actual subsequence
Time complexity is O(n log n) because each of n elements does one binary search; space is O(n)
Lower bound gives strictly increasing; upper bound gives non-decreasing
Reconstructing the actual subsequence requires parent pointers alongside the tails array

s1_definition.oneliner: Keep smallest tails; binary-search the slot; the tails array length is the LIS length.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS)** – the longest subsequence of an array where every element is strictly greater than the previous one (elements need not be contiguous).
- **Tails array** – `tails[k]` holds the smallest possible tail value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1.
- **Binary search** – for each number, find the leftmost tail that is >= the number; replace it (or append if larger than all tails).
- **Invariant** – the tails array is always sorted, which enables binary search.
- **Complexity** – O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
- **Reconstruction** – tails does not store the actual LIS; parent pointers are needed to recover it.
s1_definition.analogy: A portfolio analyst at the National Bank of India scans a daily stream of closing prices and tracks the longest run of strictly rising prices, not necessarily on consecutive days. She keeps a shelf of candidate runs ordered by their smallest ending value and slots each new price into the tightest fit, which keeps every run as extendable as possible for future prices.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Patience Sort: LIS in O(n log n)

  Input prices: [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]

  tails = []

  x=10  → append       tails = [10]
  x=9   → replace @0   tails = [9]
  x=2   → replace @0   tails = [2]
  x=5   → append       tails = [2, 5]
  x=3   → replace @1   tails = [2, 3]
  x=7   → append       tails = [2, 3, 7]
  x=101 → append       tails = [2, 3, 7, 101]
  x=18  → replace @3   tails = [2, 3, 7, 18]

  Answer: tails.size() = 4
  (tails is always sorted → binary search valid)
  (tails ≠ actual LIS, just a length device)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Increasing Subsequence in O(n log n) time uses the patience sorting technique. You maintain a tails array where the entry at index k holds the smallest possible tail value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1. For each number you binary-search the first tail that is >= the number; if there is none you append because it extends the longest run, otherwise you replace that tail because a smaller tail keeps future extension easier.

The tails array stays sorted at all times, which is what makes the binary search valid. After processing all numbers, the length of tails equals the LIS length. It is important to understand that tails is not the actual subsequence, only a length device; rebuilding the real subsequence needs parent pointers.

Using the lower bound gives a strictly increasing result, while the upper bound allows equal values for a non-decreasing variant. The naive O(n squared) DP is conceptually simpler but too slow for large inputs, so the binary search approach is the standard interview answer.

At the National Bank of India, the portfolio desk needed the longest stretch of rising closing prices to judge momentum, and those rising days did not have to be consecutive. The patience-sorting method delivered the answer on multi-year daily histories in O(n log n) time.

Remember one sentence: keep the smallest tails, binary-search each new element into them, and the tails array length is the LIS length.
